chief_complaint: confusion, headaches, dizziness, sleep disturbances, and memory difficulty 2 weeks after football concussion (Post-Concussion Syndrome)
hpi_details: 19M college varsity football player presents to sports rehabilitation clinic 14 days after sustaining a helmet-to-helmet hit during a game. Experienced immediate disorientation and brief retrograde amnesia without loss of consciousness, and was removed from play after failing sideline screening. Two weeks later, he continues to suffer from daily throbbing headaches, dizziness when changing positions, sensitivity to fluorescent lights and computer screens, brain fog, poor concentration during lectures, and irritability. Has severe difficulty sleeping.
ideas: frustrated and anxious because his symptoms are preventing him from studying for college midterm exams
concerns: desperate to get clearance to return to football practice next week before the championship game
expectations: wants specialized concussion physical therapy and medications to clear his brain fog fast
pmh: One prior mild sports concussion in high school (recovered in 7 days)

available_results.value: No acute intracranial hemorrhage, mass effect, or skull fracture
available_results.collected_at: At the initial injury 14 days before today's encounter

clinical_knowledge.topic: Post-Concussion Syndrome (Persistent Post-Concussive Symptoms / Mild Traumatic Brain Injury mTBI) with prominent Vestibulocochlear and Oculomotor dysfunction evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Post-Concussion Syndrome (Persistent Post-Concussive Symptoms / Mild Traumatic Brain Injury mTBI) with prominent Vestibulocochlear and Oculomotor dysfunction is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes withholding return-to-play clearance, graduated symptom-limited activity, and targeted vestibular/oculomotor rehabilitation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: confusion, headaches, dizziness, sleep disturbances, and memory difficulty 2 weeks after football concussion (Post-Concussion Syndrome)

Key HPI features: 19M college varsity football player presents to sports rehabilitation clinic 14 days after sustaining a helmet-to-helmet hit during a game. Experienced immediate disorientation and brief retrograde amnesia without loss of consciousness, and was removed from play after failing sideline screening. Two weeks later, he continues to suffer from daily throbbing headaches, dizziness when changing positions, sensitivity to fluorescent lights and computer screens, brain fog, poor concentration during lectures, and irritability. Has severe difficulty sleeping.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 68, BP 118/76. Comprehensive neurological examination reveals normal cranial nerves, normal 5/5 strength, and normal reflexes without focal deficits. Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening (VOMS) is highly provocative: smooth pursuit, horizontal/vertical saccades, and Vestibular-Ocular Reflex (VOR) testing induce marked dizziness, headache exacerbation, and nausea. Balance testing via the Balance Error Scoring System (BESS) demonstrates 6 errors on single-leg and tandem foam stances. Standardized assessment using the Post-Concussion Symptom Scale (PCSS) reveals moderate-to-severe symptom burden (score 42/126 across headache, photophobia, sleep disturbance, and cognitive fatigue). Head CT from initial injury was normal.
Relevant background/PMH: One prior mild sports concussion in high school (recovered in 7 days)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Post-Concussion Syndrome (Persistent Post-Concussive Symptoms / Mild Traumatic Brain Injury mTBI) with prominent Vestibulocochlear and Oculomotor dysfunction.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Soft tissue strain without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Severe progressive motor deficit.
management_principles: Return-to-Play MANDATE: strictly withhold medical clearance for collision sports or physical exertion

Withhold clearance for contact or collision sport. After an initial 24-48 hours of relative rest, begin symptom-limited activity and sub-symptom aerobic exercise; progress through a graduated return-to-sport protocol, with no return to activities carrying risk of head impact until symptoms and cognitive function have resolved and exertion is tolerated.
Rehabilitation therapy: refer immediately to PM&R Concussion Rehabilitation: Vestibular Physical Therapy (gaze stabilization exercises, habituation for dizziness) and Oculomotor Vision Therapy
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.assessment: Post-Concussion Syndrome (Persistent Post-Concussive Symptoms / Mild Traumatic Brain Injury mTBI) with prominent Vestibulocochlear and Oculomotor dysfunction.
reference_soap.plan: Do not clear the athlete for contact or collision sport. After 24-48 hours of relative rest, use clinician-supervised, symptom-limited activity and a graduated return-to-learn/return-to-sport progression; no head-impact risk until symptoms and cognition have resolved and exertion is tolerated. Refer for vestibular or oculomotor rehabilitation when targeted assessment confirms persistent deficits, and coordinate temporary academic accommodations. Obtain urgent emergency assessment for worsening or severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, increasing confusion, focal weakness/numbness, unequal pupils, or deteriorating consciousness.

learning_objectives: Administer and interpret validated clinical concussion assessments including the Vestibular/Ocular Motor Screening (VOMS) and Balance Error Scoring System (BESS) to identify specific symptom generators

Enforce the absolute clinical rule against premature return to collision sports while any concussive symptoms persist at rest or with exertion, mitigating the fatal risk of Second Impact Syndrome (diffuse malignant cerebral swelling)

Outline the strict 6-stage international consensus graduated Return-to-Play protocol (Stage 1 symptom-limited rest, Stage 2 light aerobic exercise, Stage 3 sport-specific exercise, Stage 4 non-contact training drills, Stage 5 full contact practice following medical clearance, Stage 6 return to game play)

Prescribe targeted multidisciplinary PM&R interventions including Vestibular Physical Therapy and cognitive academic accommodations (Return-to-Learn) rather than recommending prolonged dark-room isolation (cocooning)

teaching.one_liner: Physical medicine presentation involving confusion, headaches, dizziness, sleep disturbances, and memory difficulty 2 weeks after football concussion (Post-Concussion Syndrome).
red_flags: Worsening or severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizure, or increasing confusion
Focal weakness/numbness, unequal pupils, or deteriorating consciousness

must_ask.say: Can you describe how the hit to your head happened, and did you lose consciousness or have any memory loss?
What do your headaches feel like, and are they made worse by bright lights or looking at screens?
Do you feel dizzy or off-balance when you change position, like standing up quickly?
Have you had trouble concentrating, remembering things, or sleeping since the injury?
Have you had any vomiting, seizures, worsening headache, or weakness since the injury?
